items.title: Quick Automate (Automate business processes with human review) | AWS Quick: Zero to Hero 12
items.summary: Level 200. A handout on Quick Automate in AWS Quick: automate long processes that cross teams and systems, with human review. It follows a fictional learning session: read each registration, check the room booking, get the approval of the approver, and send a confirmation email. It covers when to use Quick Automate instead of Quick Flows, the planning agent, the UI agent, and custom agents, three ways to build (from a sample, from words, from scratch), the four panes of the canvas, and testing with Run and Debug. It also covers tasks for people (forms and chat) and the states of a case, deploying a committed version, monitoring in Overview, Runs, Cases, and Amazon CloudWatch, the APIs that start and check runs, export and import across groups, accounts, and Regions, and the Viewer, Contributor, and Owner roles and credentials. Quick Automate is not on Free or Plus accounts created at aws.com/quick. The pricing page lists Enterprise and the FAQs also list Professional, so the deck shows both. Screens are from the web app in the Tokyo Region with the English display language, and the flow figures are drawn from the public documentation. The appendix lists the actions, a glossary, and the sources. Based on the public documentation and screens as of November 2026. Deck 12 (Let it run) of the series AWS Quick: Zero to Hero.

items.title: Agents and skills (Give agents roles and procedures, plus memory) | AWS Quick: Zero to Hero 06
items.summary: Level 200. How to give agents in AWS Quick their roles and procedures, for business users who already use AWS Quick on the web. It explains what an agent is (a worker with set instructions, materials, and tools), the built-in Quick and custom chat agents, and whether to set the materials or leave them open. It walks through building a chat agent on the web (describing its purpose, the settings screen, reference documents and knowledge sources) and sharing it with the Owner or Viewer role, with screens captured in English. It then covers skills in the desktop app: what a skill is, the two stages in which agents load skills, building a skill from chat, a file, or a folder, drafts, Try it, publishing and sharing, and official skills in Add to Quick. It ends with memory: viewing and deleting it on the web, and editing it on desktop. The running scenario is a team's monthly learning session. The appendix has agent and skill limits, a glossary, and sources. Based on public documentation and screens as of November 2026. Deck 06 (Go deeper) of the series AWS Quick: Zero to Hero.

items.title: Keep improving (Recommendations and A/B tests) | Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro 09
items.summary: Level 300. A made-up online shop's help-desk agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime reads its prompt from a configuration bundle, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore optimization turns its real records into a prompt recommendation; because the recommendation broke a shop rule to raise its target score, a person fixes that one line, saves it as a new bundle version, and compares three versions on the same 12 cases with batch evaluation. An A/B test through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway then splits 48 scripted customer sessions between the current version and the fixed one, finds no significant difference, and is paused, all shown with real output and flow figures; this is the third deck of the Observe and improve part of Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro, after decks 07 and 08.

items.title: Evaluate it (Score real sessions with AgentCore Evaluations) | Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro 08
items.summary: This Level 300 deck shows how to evaluate an agent that can give a different answer to the same request: cases built from real failures, scoring by the outcome with the tool order checked only where it matters, and the built-in and custom evaluators of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations with its three ways to run (on-demand, online and batch). On the help desk agent of a made-up online electronics shop, it scores one inquiry on the spot, keeps scoring production with an online evaluation, and compares two versions of the instructions in batch with references, shown with figures of what happened and real terminal output, as deck 08 (Observe and improve) of the series Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro.

items.title: See what it did (Traces and Amazon CloudWatch) | Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro 07
items.summary: This Level 300 deck shows how to follow what a help desk agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime did: the shape of its records (sessions, traces, spans, logs and metrics), how AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) sends them to Amazon CloudWatch in OpenTelemetry format with no code added, where they are kept, and how to protect the inquiry text they hold. With real terminal lines from the deck 01 help desk, it checks Transaction Search, lists and saves a trace with the AgentCore CLI, draws it as a span tree, finds a failure in the ERROR logs and counts calls and errors, and then covers where the time goes, alarms, passing traceparent and the session ID from the caller, cross-account monitoring, a weekly reading habit that turns odd records into evaluation cases, CloudWatch costs, and where to look first.

items.title: Connect tools (Turn APIs and MCP servers into tools with Gateway) | Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro 04
items.summary: This Level 300 deck shows why an agent picks the wrong tool when similar tools pile up, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway puts a shop's three AWS Lambda functions behind one MCP endpoint with IAM inbound auth and semantic tool search, drawn with the official AWS icons. It then takes the help desk agent of a made-up online electronics shop through the AgentCore CLI (add gateway, add gateway-target, deploy to the Tokyo Region, invoke) with real terminal output, and checks tool names, descriptions, error results, rate limits and prices against the AgentCore documentation, as deck 04 (Build it out) of the series Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro.

items.title: Get more from Runtime (Sessions, versions and endpoints, and long-running tasks) | Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro 02
items.summary: This Level 300 deck takes the help desk agent of a made-up online electronics shop, deployed to AgentCore Runtime in deck 01, and makes it ready for many users: a dedicated microVM for each session with the session ID made and kept by the caller, the session life cycle (Active, Idle, Stopped, 15 minutes idle and 8 hours by default), streamed answers, and long-running tasks that return a receipt at once and keep working in a back thread with add_async_task while /ping says HealthyBusy. It then shows versions and named endpoints (try a new version on a test endpoint, then move production), inbound auth with IAM or JWT, the protocols, microVM V1 and V2 and Instances, zip or container, and a clean-up that keeps the versions, with figures that use the official AWS icons and real terminal screens, as deck 02 (Get started) of the series Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro.

items.title: How AgentCore works (The map of services, and your first deploy) | Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro 01
items.summary: This Level 300 deck shows why an agent that runs on one laptop needs isolation, memory, authentication and a record of its actions once many people use it, and maps the 13 services of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that cover them and the two ways to deploy (a code-based agent on AgentCore Runtime, or a managed harness), with figures that use the official AWS icons. It then takes the help desk agent of a made-up online electronics shop through the AgentCore CLI (create, dev with the local Agent Inspector, deploy to the Tokyo Region, invoke, logs and status), with an architecture diagram of what deploy makes, what stays after clean up and how the cost is counted, as deck 01 (Get started) of the series Learn Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Kiro.
